title: Will Your Ex Come Back?

options.label: We both did, more or less
It faded out, or it's complicated

intake.question: How long ago did it end?
What do you want right now, honestly?

plan.title: How it ended, and what the clock says
Why you still check their profile
Too much of one thing, none of another
Will they come back? No sugar-coating
What you do now (Yeon wrote a plan)

strong.text:
Yeon: Strong chart, so let's talk about your part. You don't lose arguments. You win them. Every single one.

Bom: Winning a fight and keeping a person are two different sports.

Yeon: You were so busy being right you didn't notice them getting quieter.

Think of one fight you "won". Now replay it from their side, in one sentence. That sentence is probably closer to why it ended than anything they said at the end.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You won every argument. Look where it got you. Single, and correct.

weak.text:
Bom: Your chart runs soft. You gave and gave, and somewhere in there you stopped saying what you needed.

Yeon: Then one day you were resentful and they had no idea why. Because you never told them.

Bom: That's not a failure of love. It's a failure of volume.

Name one thing you needed and never said out loud. Just one. Keep it. It's the first line of your next relationship.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You loved quietly. Next time, love a little louder.

strong.text:
Strong chart, so you run this pattern on willpower. New gym plan by Wednesday. New project by Friday. Posts that say "doing great" in a very calm font.

Bom: People keep telling you that you seem fine. You keep taking it as a compliment.

Yeon: Fine isn't a feeling. It's a press release.

Bom: You can outrun a feeling for months. It just waits, then shows up as you snapping at a barista for saying "no worries" in their exact voice.

Yeon: You don't need to slow your whole life down. Give the plan one exit. One friend who's allowed to ask "no, how are you actually?" and get a real answer.

Bom: Next page: who ended it, and how long ago. The clock says more about you than you'd think.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Strong isn't the same as healed. Who gets the real version?

weak.text:
Softer chart, so you run this pattern through other people. You've told the story to four friends, two group chats and one coworker who did not ask.

Yeon: That's not processing. That's a poll.

Bom: You lean on people because leaning is how you heal. That part is right.

Yeon: The problem is you've collected so many opinions you can't hear your own. You've even started believing their version of the breakup. The ex's version. Why.

Bom: Pick two people whose judgment you trust. Mute the chat that turned your breakup into a weekly series. Keep one small thing that's only yours: the same walk, a page in a notebook, a song nobody else gets to hear.

Yeon: Now. You told us who ended it and when. Let's see what that says. Next page.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Two trusted people. Everyone else gets a thank-you and the mute button.

strong.text:
Strong chart, so the pull has a competitive streak. You don't only miss them. You want the last word. You want proof you were the bigger loss.

Yeon: That's why checking feels like research. You're not pining. You're gathering evidence.

Bom: Next time you open their profile, notice what you're hoping to find. Them sad? Them fine, so you can stop worrying? A new person in the background of slide three?

Yeon: Each answer means something different. None of them means "text them".

Bom: You're good at rules. So set one, once: no checking on weeknights, or none at all for thirty days. You already have the willpower. Aim it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Trying to win the breakup is still being in it. Pick a different sport.

weak.text:
Softer chart, so the pull is about reassurance. One look at their story is a tiny dose of contact. Proof the connection still exists, even one way.

Bom: The catch is that every look also reopens "was I enough?", and at night your chart answers that one cruelly.

Yeon: Notice when it happens. It's never 11am after a good lunch. It's 11pm, tired, alone, slightly hungry.

Bom: So this is a logistics problem, not a discipline problem. Put something else in that slot. A call with someone who likes you. The show you're halfway through. The charger in the kitchen.

Yeon: Wanting comfort isn't weak. Getting it from a source that costs you tomorrow morning is just bad budgeting.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Tired and alone is when it hits. Put something kinder in that slot.

strong.text:
Here's the strong-chart part. If a second chance ever came up, you could make it work by effort. You can make most things work by effort.

Yeon: The real question is whether you'd let it be different. Strong charts restart relationships from the exact spot they ended. Just with better arguments.

Bom: Make a list. What you'd change in you. What you'd need from them. Which of those you can check without asking anybody.

Yeon: If the whole list is their changes, you have your answer about timing. From your side, anyway.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: If round two is "same me, sharper points", rethink round two.

weak.text:
Here's the soft-chart part. When support is thin, the person who once made you feel steady starts to look like the only steady thing on earth.

Bom: That's why "will they come back" feels enormous, like your footing depends on it. It doesn't. It only feels that way at 1am.

Yeon: Ask what you're actually missing. Them? Or being held?

Bom: If it's the second, a lot of that can be rebuilt with friends, routine and real sleep. And you'll think far more clearly about the first once you have.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Some of what you miss can come from friends, sleep and your own routine. Only part of it needs them.

strong.text:
A note for strong charts. Your instinct on that first reply is to take control. Set the terms. Deliver the summary. Ask the pointed question.

Bom: It feels like self-respect.

Yeon: To them it feels like being called into a meeting with HR.

Bom: Let the first reply be short and warm, and leave room for them to say why they wrote. You can be clear later.

Yeon: Try: "Good to hear from you. What made you reach out?" Then actually wait. Listening first costs you nothing.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Short and warm first. You can be clear in message two.

weak.text:
A note for softer charts. Your instinct is to say yes to whatever they offer. Coffee, a call, a vague "let's see". Because any contact feels better than none.

Yeon: Slow. Down.

Bom: Wait a few hours. Write your reply somewhere other than the chat box. Read it back: does it say what you want, or only what keeps them talking?

Yeon: Try: "I'm glad you wrote. I need a day to think about how I want to answer." Protects you, closes nothing.

Bom: People who matter can wait a day.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Draft it in your notes app, not the chat. Thumbs are not decision makers.

strong.text:
One more thing for strong charts: give the restlessness a job. You've got more drive than you know what to do with right now, and unused drive turns into replaying.

Yeon: Pick one project with a finish line inside six weeks. A course. A room you repaint. A race. The stack of books you've been pretending to read.

Bom: Something where you can see the progress. It beats arguing with a memory.

Yeon: And while you're at it, one soft skill, on purpose: ask a friend how they are, then ask a second question before you talk about yourself.

Bom: Yes, a second question. Yeon is also practising this.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your drive needs a project with a finish line. Your ex doesn't count as one.

weak.text:
One more thing for softer charts: rebuild your supports before you test them.

Bom: Sleep before strategy. Food before big talks. Old friends before new people.

Yeon: Make a short list of what refills you. Treat it like a daily habit, not a reward you earn for good behaviour.

Bom: Keep commitments small for a few weeks. Say no without a paragraph of reasons.

Yeon: Nobody needs a busy, impressive recovery from you. A quiet one counts.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rest, meals, your people. The big decisions can wait their turn.

peer_strong.text:
There's a lot of {dm_el} in your chart, which is your own element. Basically, your chart is a room full of you.

Yeon: Which explains why every argument had two lawyers and no judge.

Bom: You're self-reliant to a fault. You never fully handed over the wheel, so it felt like two people negotiating instead of one couple deciding.

Yeon: You also competed with them. Who apologised more. Who gave up more. Who's coping better right now, judging by stories.

Bom: The upside is real: you rarely stay knocked down. The work is learning that needing someone doesn't cancel your independence. (Saju calls this the peer family: siblings, rivals, your own reflection.)

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: So much of you in there. Not much space left for anyone else.

output_strong.text:
Lots of {heavy_el} in your chart, the element your {dm_el} makes. Plain English: you're good with words, and you use them. All of them.

Bom: You probably said a lot in this relationship, and said it well.

Yeon: You also said the sharp version. The clever one. The line with a perfect landing that you could never take back.

Bom: This side of you also hates being managed. Anyone who tried to run your schedule met a wall, on principle.

Yeon: Right now it wants to explain the breakup to everyone, post the playlist, and write The Long Message.

Bom: Let it make something instead. A song, a letter you keep, a sketchbook. The feeling is real. It just shouldn't be aimed at them. (Saju calls this the output family: talent and expression.)

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el}: great with words. Also great at sending them at midnight.

wealth_strong.text:
Lots of {heavy_el} in your chart, the element your {dm_el} shapes and steers. Translation: you're the one who organised everything.

Yeon: The trips. The lease. The five-year idea in a shared note they never opened.

Bom: Saju calls this the wealth family. It's less about money than about what you reach for and run.

Yeon: Which means the breakup might feel like a failed project as much as a lost person. Notice that. A person isn't a result.

Bom: If you want to understand what happened, look for the moments you were managing them instead of meeting them. Steering a story they hadn't signed up for.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You held all the plans together. That was love too. Just not the whole of it.

power_strong.text:
Lots of {heavy_el} in your chart, the element that keeps your {dm_el} in line. There's a referee living in you, and it takes the job very seriously.

Bom: You meant every promise. You take commitment more seriously than most people you know.

Yeon: You also held the relationship to a standard, and yourself to a stricter one, until it felt more like an exam than a home.

Bom: After a breakup the referee becomes a judge. First: what did I do wrong. Then: what did they do wrong. Then: am I even allowed to feel this bad.

Yeon: Close the courtroom for the night. Some things end because two decent people wanted different lives. No ruling required. (Saju calls this the power family: rules, duty, pressure.)

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your inner referee wants a verdict. Some breakups end in a draw.

resource_strong.text:
Lots of {heavy_el} in your chart, the element that feeds your {dm_el}. You're thoughtful, fine on your own, slow to panic.

Yeon: You're also the person who read four articles on attachment styles this week and diagnosed you both.

Bom: You can think a feeling to death. Understanding feels safer than doing.

Yeon: You've understood this breakup from every angle. You could teach a module on it. You have done zero things about it.

Bom: One small physical move this week. Return their things. Archive the chat. Book the haircut. (Saju calls this the resource family: care, learning, the mother element.)

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Enough thinking for now. One small action this week beats ten more theories.

output_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} pours out. On a softer chart that drains more than it refills. Like a phone on 9% running every app.

Bom: You gave a lot. Time, favours, attention, long supportive texts. It felt natural, until you noticed you were tired all the time.

Yeon: And now there's nothing left to process the breakup with. You spent it all on them.

Bom: Stop producing for a while. No long explanations, no posts, no checking that everyone's okay with how it ended.

Yeon: Let people bring you things for once. Yes, you have to say thank you and not repay it within the hour.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You poured out so much. Let the tank refill before you explain anything.

wealth_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} tries to hold and manage. Old saju books have a phrase for this: heavy wealth, light self. A lot to carry, not much behind you to carry it with.

Yeon: So you took responsibility for the whole relationship. Its moods, its plans, its survival. On one arm.

Bom: While quietly running on empty.

Yeon: If part of you feels relieved it's over, and guilty about the relief, that's this.

Bom: Let the relief be okay. Your job right now isn't to rescue anything. It's to put down what was never yours alone.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Carrying a relationship single-handed isn't loyalty. It's a sprain.

power_weak.text:
Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element that pushes on your {dm_el}. On a softer chart, that's heavy pressure on a light frame.

Bom: You spent the relationship trying to be acceptable. Checking your tone. Smoothing things over before they even happened.

Yeon: Now that pressure has a voice. It sounds like a disappointed teacher reading your report out loud.

Bom: It's loud. It isn't a fact.

Yeon: Lower the bar this month, on purpose. Rest. Kind people. Anyone who doesn't grade you. You'll think better without the whistle.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: That strict voice in your head isn't the truth. It's just loud.

rooted_on_paper.text:
What that means for this breakup: from outside you look steady. Opinions, a plan, a calm face. Underneath it's wobblier, because your support is scattered instead of rooted.

Yeon: That's why you're sure about everything at 2pm and doubting your whole personality by midnight.

Bom: Neither mood is lying. One is the plenty people see. The other is the root you don't have yet.

Yeon: House rule: no decisions after dark. Decide at noon, after food, ideally after talking to someone who knows you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Confident in daylight, doubting after dark. Big calls happen at lunchtime.

output_strong.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the outlet, the way feelings leave the building. A strong chart with no outlet is a pressure cooker.

Yeon: So it all comes out at once. Usually about the dishwasher, while the real thing stays unsaid.

Bom: You probably held the important stuff in until it boiled over. That pattern matters more than any single fight.

Yeon: Schedule smaller vents. One true sentence a day to someone safe. Write instead of rehearsing. Run until something loosens.

Bom: Expression is a skill. You can learn it like you learned everything else.

Yeon: Okay. Deep breath. The question you actually came here for is next.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No {miss_el} means no outlet. Let it out in small doses before the lid blows.

wealth_strong.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the target, the part of life you aim at and shape.

Bom: So you've got plenty of drive and not always a clear place to point it.

Yeon: Which is how a relationship becomes The Place. And when it ends, all that force is just standing in your kitchen with nowhere to go.

Bom: Borrow some on purpose. One thing you'll finish. One thing you'll fix. One thing you'll build.

Yeon: A shelf to assemble beats a person to fix. Every time.

Bom: Now the big question. Yeon promised to be gentle. Yeon was lying. Next page.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Spare drive needs a target. Flat-pack furniture is right there.

power_strong.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the referee. A strong chart with no referee writes its own rules and edits them when it feels like it.

Yeon: Which is why "I didn't think it was a big deal" has left your mouth more than once.

Bom: It's freedom. It can also mean you missed it when you crossed a line, or when one of their lines mattered more than you thought.

Yeon: Borrow structure from outside. One friend who's allowed to call you out. A few promises to yourself, written down, kept.

Bom: Outside boundaries feel strange at first. Then they start to feel like respect.

Yeon: Right. Will they come back. Let's do it properly. Next.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No referee in your chart. So borrow one: a friend who'll tell you straight.

resource_strong.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the element that looks after you and teaches you to rest. You're strong without it, which usually means you learned to look after yourself early.

Bom: The cost: being cared for feels awkward. You were easier to love than to comfort.

Yeon: Someone asks if you're okay and you say "I'm fine" so fast it leaves skid marks.

Bom: Borrow it on purpose. Let someone cook for you. Take the advice you'd give a friend. Sleep in without earning it first.

Yeon: Now, the question you've been scrolling toward this whole time. Next page.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You're allowed to be looked after without filing a request first.

output_weak.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's how feelings get out. On a softer chart that's partly protective: you don't leak yourself into every conversation.

Bom: The downside is hurt gets stored instead of said. Stored hurt comes back later as tiredness you can't explain.

Yeon: You don't need a big outlet. You'd hate a big outlet.

Bom: Small ones, often. A voice note to a friend. Two lines in a journal. A song sung badly in the car.

Yeon: Okay. The question. The real one. Turn the page.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Hurt you never say still finds a way out. Let it out gently, a bit at a time.

wealth_weak.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the urge to grab hold of results. On a softer chart, that's quietly a blessing. You're less likely to chase.

Yeon: The risk goes the other way. Drifting. Letting things happen to you. Including, possibly, the ending.

Bom: Borrow a little of that grab in tiny amounts. One clear wish, said out loud. One small thing you decide instead of accept.

Yeon: Start with lunch. Choose it yourself, nobody consulted. Work up from there.

Bom: Next, the question you came here with. We'll answer it straight.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Practise choosing on sandwiches. Then on bigger things. Then on people.

power_weak.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's outside pressure and rules. For a softer chart, mostly good news: one less thing leaning on you.

Bom: It can also mean you never learned to ask for structure. So you had none, or you borrowed your partner's. And theirs left with them.

Yeon: Hence the 3am cereal and texting at hours that should be illegal.

Bom: Build a light version of your own. A bedtime. One standing plan a week. A rule about late-night texting.

Yeon: Structure you pick isn't pressure. It's a handrail. Hold on to it, because the next chapter is the big one.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No pressure element. Good. Pick one gentle rule and let it hold you up.

resource_weak.text:
No {miss_el} in the chart we can see. For your {dm_el}, that's the element that feeds you directly.

Bom: Which explains why support matters so much to you, and why losing someone who felt like home knocked you flat.

Yeon: It's not a flaw. Your chart just doesn't come with its own supply. Batteries not included.

Bom: So you build the supply from outside, on purpose. Kind people. Rest you don't apologise for. Something new you're learning that's only yours.

Yeon: Collect sources. One person was never meant to be all of them. Next page: the question.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: One source of comfort is fragile. Five is a support system. Start collecting.

none_strong.text:
All five elements turn up somewhere in your chart, even if a few are hiding. On a strong chart that gives you range. Blunt and tender. Practical and dreamy.

Yeon: You've been all of those in this relationship. Sometimes before lunch.

Bom: The risk with range is picking whichever mode wins the argument in the moment.

Yeon: When you think about them now, check who's talking. Fight-mode you tells one story. Missing-them-at-2am you tells another.

Bom: Neither is the whole picture. Hold both, and let's get to what you actually came here for.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: All five elements. Including the one that just wants to win.

none_weak.text:
All five elements turn up somewhere in your chart, even if a few are hiding. On a softer chart that means you have more tools than you think. What you're short on is root, not range.

Bom: You can comfort, plan, speak, finish and rest. You just tire faster than most.

Yeon: So stop trying to use all five tools on the same Tuesday.

Bom: Today, maybe it's rest. Tomorrow, maybe it's the conversation you've been dodging. One at a time is plenty.

Yeon: Okay. Will they come back? Next page. No sugar.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: A full toolbox doesn't mean using every tool today.

resource.title: Your refill: {helper_el}
resource.text:
Every chart has one element that brings it back to level. For a softer {dm_el} chart, it's the one that feeds you. For you, that's {helper_el}.

Bom: This is the most practical paragraph in your whole reading. Screenshot it.

Yeon: When you feel scattered, you don't need another insight about them. You need more {helper_el} in your actual days.

Bom: Feed the root, stop trimming the branches. When the root's fed, the questions about them get quieter, and your judgment comes back.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your refill is {helper_el}. Less analysis of them, more of that.

peer.title: Your refill: {helper_el}, your own element
peer.text:
Every chart has one element that brings it back to level. Yours already has plenty of comfort on paper, so what helps most is your own, {helper_el}.

Yeon: Meaning: your people. Not new people. The ones who knew you before this relationship and will know you after it.

Bom: And things that remind you who you are without anyone else's input.

Yeon: You don't need more advice. You've had advice. You need someone standing next to you, on your level, on your side.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your refill is your own element, {helper_el}. Call the friends who knew you first.

output.title: Your release valve: {helper_el}
output.text:
Every chart has one element that brings it back to level. A strong {dm_el} chart doesn't need more support. It needs a way to let the strength out. For you, that's {helper_el}.

Yeon: So no, your advice isn't "rest and reflect". You've reflected. You've reflected so hard there's a dent.

Bom: It's expression and motion. Sitting still with a chart like yours turns into replaying, and replaying turns into a story on loop.

Yeon: Move. Make. Finish things. Same force, but it comes out as something you'll be proud of in a month.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your release valve is {helper_el}. Translation: stop stewing, start doing.

wealth.title: Something with edges: {helper_el}
wealth.text:
Every chart has one element that brings it back to level. Yours is strong and already pours plenty out, so what helps most is {helper_el}, the thing your chart likes to work on and shape.

Bom: Plain version: you need targets. Tasks with edges. Things you can finish and point at.

Yeon: A list of three things you can tick off by Friday will calm you more than a long talk about feelings. At first. Don't tell Bom I said that.

Bom: I heard that. The talk can come later, once the restlessness has somewhere to land.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your balancing element is {helper_el}. Give the restlessness a target.

wood.text:
{helper_el}, in real life: green things and growth. Walks under trees. A plant on the windowsill you actually water. A skill at beginner level. Plans that point forward.

Bom: It's the element of starting. So start something small that isn't about them at all.

Yeon: Coming up: them. Including what to do if they suddenly text.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood looks like walks, plants and new beginnings. Go green for a while.

fire.text:
{helper_el}, in real life: warmth and people. Morning sun on your face. Dinners with friends who make you laugh with your mouth full. Saying the thing out loud instead of thinking it. Music loud enough to feel in your ribs.

Bom: It's the element of being seen. So let yourself be seen by people who are glad to see you.

Yeon: Speaking of being seen. Up next: them, and what to do if they come knocking.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire looks like sunlight, laughing, and saying it with your actual mouth. Go where it's warm.

earth.text:
{helper_el}, in real life: routine and home. Meals at the same time. The same bedtime. Something slow in the oven. A walk on the same route. Friends you can sit with in silence, and it's fine.

Yeon: Boring is the plan. Stick to it daily.

Bom: Keep things simple and predictable for a while. Then turn the page, because next it's about them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth looks like regular meals and early nights. Unexciting, and it works.

metal.text:
{helper_el}, in real life: edges and order. Clearing one drawer. Archiving the chat. A clean desk. A firm no. Finishing the thing you started in March.

Bom: It's the harvest element: cut what's done so the rest can breathe. Tidy one physical space and notice how much quieter your head gets.

Yeon: Quiet head, good. You'll need it for what's next: them, and what happens if they reach out.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal means edges. Clear the drawer. Finish the thing.

water.text:
{helper_el}, in real life: rest and depth. Long sleep. Baths. Swims. Evenings with nothing planned. Reading. Slow conversations that run past midnight on purpose.

Yeon: Looking lazy counts as recovery. Bom made me say that.

Bom: Water is winter, when things restore underground. Let yourself look like you're doing nothing. Next page, we talk about them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water looks like sleep and slow evenings. Resting counts as doing something.

rat.text: The Rat sits closest to your heart: clever, private, awake at night. You probably saw the cracks early and kept the information to yourself. In the next one, share the intel.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rat heart: you clocked every warning sign. Then filed it under "later".

ox.text: The Ox guards your heart: loyal, slow, steady. You stayed longer than made sense because leaving felt like breaking a promise. Loyalty is beautiful. So is knowing when it's done.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ox heart: you don't leave easily. That's why this hurts so much.

tiger.text: The Tiger sits in your heart: brave, proud, independent. You'd rather suffer in private than look like you're begging. Wanting them back isn't weakness. Pretending you don't care is just armour.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Tiger heart: you'd rather lose them than lose face. Noted.

rabbit.text: The Rabbit lives close to your heart: gentle, charming, conflict-shy. You kept things smooth until smooth stopped being honest. Next time, one small fight early saves one big ending later.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rabbit heart: keeping the peace isn't the same as having it.

dragon.text: The Dragon guards your heart: big dreams, big expectations. You wanted something legendary, and anything less felt like settling. Some of that is standards. Some of it is a story nobody could live up to.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Dragon heart: you wanted an epic. They wanted a Tuesday.

snake.text: The Snake sits closest to your heart: intuitive, private, strategic. You read them perfectly and showed them very little. They loved someone they never fully saw.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Snake heart: you saw everything. They saw a closed door.

horse.text: The Horse lives in your heart: passionate, restless, freedom first. When it felt like a fence, you ran, even if you only ran in your head. The right person won't feel like a fence.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Horse heart: you need open fields. That was always allowed.

goat.text: The Goat guards your heart: gentle, homey, needs reassurance. You needed to hear "we're okay" more than they said it. Next time, ask for it. Plainly. It's not too much.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Goat heart: needing reassurance isn't needy. It's how you're built.

monkey.text: The Monkey sits in your heart: clever, playful, bores easily. The banter was the best part, and when the banter faded you wondered what was left. Fun matters. So does what's under it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Monkey heart: you miss the jokes more than the person. Be honest.

rooster.text: The Rooster guards your heart: proud, precise, critical. You saw what was wrong and said so, often. You were usually right. Being right was lonely by the end.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rooster heart: you had notes. On everything. They got tired of notes.

dog.text: The Dog lives close to your heart: loyal, protective, principled. You stayed loyal past the point it was good for you. That loyalty is a gift. Give it to someone who guards it back.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Dog heart: so loyal. Next time, to someone who's loyal back.

pig.text: The Pig sits in your heart: sweet, generous, trusting. You gave second chances like party favours. Kindness isn't the mistake. Ignoring your own red flags is.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Pig heart: you forgave things you should've at least mentioned.

day_branch_heading: Who you let in close: the {day_animal} ({day_branch})

me_strong.text:
You ended it. You'd defend that decision in court. Some nights you basically do, alone, to your ceiling.

Yeon: Then you see one photo of them looking fine at a barbecue and suddenly the case is reopened.

Bom: Being the one who left doesn't mean you stop missing them. It means there was real good in it, and you still chose.

Yeon: Right and sad. Those two have shared a flat for years.

Bom: The decision already did its job. It doesn't have to win again every Tuesday.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You ended it and you miss them. Both true. Stop calling witnesses.

me_weak.text:
You ended it. For you that took more nerve than anyone gave you credit for, because disappointing people physically hurts you.

Bom: And ever since, you've carried the guilt around like a second bag you forgot to put down.

Yeon: Quick check. Did you end it so gently they're not sure it ended? Was there a "maybe one day" in there, to soften the moment?

Bom: Kind and vague aren't the same thing. A clear ending is the gentler one, for both of you.

Yeon: You made a hard call. You're allowed to feel bad about it without un-making it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: A hard choice and real sadness can sit together. Neither means undo it.

them_strong.text:
They ended it. So you're dealing with two losses at once: them, and the steering wheel.

Yeon: Which is why there's an untitled note on your phone, four paragraphs long, with the word "actually" in it six times.

Bom: You want them to see it clearly. One conversation where it finally makes sense to them.

Yeon: Their decision wasn't a debate you lost on points. No closing argument reverses it.

Bom: You can think they got it wrong and still respect that it was theirs to make. Put your force into the part you do steer: who you are about this a year from now.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No rebuttal overturns a decision that was never put to a vote.

them_weak.text:
They ended it. And somewhere in your head, that turned into a grade. On you. In red pen.

Bom: It isn't one. A breakup tells you what one person could or couldn't do, in that relationship, at that time. That's all it can tell you.

Yeon: You've been rewinding the tape looking for the exact second you lost them. Spoiler: in every edit, you cast yourself as the problem.

Bom: Your chart reaches for that story first. It's a habit, not a fact.

Yeon: New exercise. List what you gave that was good. The coffee runs. The patience. The time you drove two hours for one dinner. Go.

Bom: It's a longer list than you think. All of it still counts.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Being left is not a verdict on you. Write down what you gave. It counted.

mutual_strong.text:
You both ended it, more or less. You've described it as "really mature, honestly". Twice this week.

Yeon: And yet some part of you is still keeping score of who agreed first.

Bom: Mutual endings sound tidy. They rarely feel tidy.

Yeon: They also leave the door looking ajar, which is catnip for a strong chart. You've half planned the reunion already. Venue included.

Bom: Remember what actually happened: two people looked at the same relationship and reached the same answer. That's rare. Take it seriously, even on days you'd rather argue with it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: The door looks open. That doesn't make it a sequel. Stop scouting venues.

mutual_weak.text:
You both ended it, more or less. So why does it feel like you're not allowed to be this sad?

Bom: Because nobody's the villain. No big fight, no story for your friends. Just a loss with no headline.

Yeon: Also, be honest. Did you agree partly so it'd be easier for them? You did, didn't you.

Bom: Agreeing that something should end doesn't stop it being a loss. Be properly sad for a while. You don't need a dramatic enough reason.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No villain, and you're still allowed to be sad. Quiet losses count too.

unclear_strong.text:
It faded out. No last fight, no final talk, nothing to push against. For a strong chart that's maddening.

Yeon: Which is why you're tempted to schedule an ending now. A big message. A summit. Possibly an agenda with numbered points.

Bom: Before you send anything, ask what you want from it.

Yeon: If it's closure, you can make that yourself. Write what ended, when you knew, and what you're keeping.

Bom: If it's another round, that's allowed too. Just be honest that that's what the message is really for.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No clear ending? Write one. It doesn't need their signature.

unclear_weak.text:
It faded out. So instead of a door, you got a question mark, and you've been living inside it.

Bom: You're still waiting for the conversation that never happened. Every "haha" from them in a group chat gets read as a maybe.

Yeon: The maybe is very expensive. You're paying rent on it every night.

Bom: You don't need them to agree it's over. You can call it finished, for now, for your own peace. If life hands you a real reason later, you can change your mind then.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Call it finished for your own peace. The maybe costs too much.

unsaid.text:
You skipped who ended it. Fine. Here's what's true however it went: one person usually sees the end first, and one person gets told.

Bom: The one who sees it coming grieves early and alone, while still sharing a sofa.

Yeon: The one who gets told grieves all at once, usually in a car park.

Bom: Work out which one you were. Privately. It changes what you need now.

Yeon: Early grievers need permission to be done. The ones who got told need time, and far more patience with themselves than they're currently giving.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Saw it coming, or got told? Different wounds, different fixes.

fresh.text:
Under a month. Very fresh. Read the rest of this gently.

Bom: Your body is still running the old schedule. The good-morning text. The Friday default. The person you'd tell about the weird thing at work.

Yeon: Every one of those habits fires, finds nobody, and you feel it in your chest. That's withdrawal, not a sign.

Bom: Big decisions about them can wait. Right now the only job is getting through the evenings.

Yeon: Speaking of evenings. Let's talk about what your thumb does in them. Next chapter.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Under a month is very fresh. Tonight's only job: get through tonight.

months.text:
One to six months. The shock's gone, the sorting has started, and everyone assumes you're fine.

Yeon: Some days you are. Then a stranger walks past in their jacket and Thursday is cancelled.

Bom: This is also when the urge to check in gets loudest, because the pain is quieter and the memories have gone soft-focus.

Yeon: Memory deletes the bad scenes first. Very flattering editor.

Bom: Keep one honest note of why it ended. Read it whenever the edited version gets convincing.

Yeon: And now, the real question. Why do you still open their profile? Turn the page.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your memory cut the bad bits. Fact-check it with your own note.

half.text:
Six to twelve months. Long enough that you think you should be over it. Short enough that you're not.

Bom: That gap feels embarrassing. It isn't. Plenty of people are still measuring their days against an old relationship at this point.

Yeon: The question has changed, though. It's not "them" anymore. It's "what have I built since?"

Bom: If the honest answer is "not much", that's where your effort goes now. A life that's growing makes the past look smaller on its own.

Yeon: Unless you're still checking their page. Which, let's discuss. Next.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Not over it by month eight? Normal. Build something new and the past shrinks.

long.text:
Over a year. And you're still reading a comic about them. So this one left a real mark.

Bom: Worth asking why this one. Often it's not only the person. It's who you were next to them, or the future that walked out with them.

Yeon: Those are separate griefs. You've been treating them as one.

Bom: Ask what you miss most. Then ask if it has to come from them. Sometimes yes. Often it's a part of your own life you can go back and get.

Yeon: Which brings us to the thing your thumb does at 1am. Next chapter.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: A year on, ask what you actually miss. Sometimes it's a version of you.

unsaid.text:
However long it's been, time is doing two jobs. Softening the memory, and building a habit of thinking about them.

Bom: The first is natural. The second you can interrupt.

Yeon: When their name pops into your head, ask one thing back: is this a feeling, or a habit?

Bom: Feelings get a minute of attention. Habits get a different thought, picked on purpose.

Yeon: And the biggest habit of all lives in your phone. Next chapter.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Feelings get a minute. Habits get a new thought.

back_strong.text:
You said you want to get back together. With your chart, wanting something turns into a plan fast. Possibly a spreadsheet.

Yeon: You can't project-manage someone's heart. And no chart can see theirs.

Bom: What you can do is make sure the person they'd meet now isn't the one they left. Put the next weeks into that. Not into them.

Yeon: If a door ever opens, you walk in different. If it doesn't, you still changed, and every relationship after this gets that version.

Bom: One habit stands in the way, though. Yeon's been dying to say it. Next page.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Want them back? Work on the you they'd meet. Not on a strategy.

back_weak.text:
You said you want to get back together. Honest question first: how much of that is them, and how much is the floor dropping out when they left?

Bom: Both are human. But going back because you feel shaky alone usually replays the same relationship, scene for scene.

Yeon: Steady yourself first. Sleep, friends, a normal week. Then check whether the want is still there.

Bom: If it is, it's a clearer want. If it fades, that tells you something too.

Yeon: Next, your blind spot. You'll recognise it immediately. Annoyingly.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Get your feet under you, then ask the question again. The answer gets clearer.

closure_strong.text:
You said you want closure. You've pictured it: one final conversation where everything gets said properly, in order, and they finally nod.

Yeon: Lovely scene. They can't play it. Most people can't hand you the answer, because they don't fully have it either.

Bom: Closure is something you can finish yourself. Write the questions you'd ask. Then answer them as honestly as you can from what you know.

Yeon: The answers won't be perfect. They'll be yours, and they won't depend on anyone's calendar.

Bom: There's a reason you need it this badly, by the way. It lives in your blind spot. Next.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You don't need their answers to close this. Your own are usually right.

closure_weak.text:
You said you want closure. Right now it feels like you need their permission to be okay.

Bom: You don't. They may never say the sentence you're waiting for, and your peace can't sit in a waiting room for it.

Yeon: Write the letter you won't send. All of it. Including the petty parts. Especially those.

Bom: Then write one line back to yourself, the thing a good friend would say. Read that line on the bad days.

Yeon: Now, the part of you that made this hurt the way it did. Next page.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Unsendable letter first. Then a kind reply, from you, to you.

move_strong.text:
You said you want to stop thinking about them. So you've been shoving the thought away. Hard. Like a door in a storm.

Yeon: How's that going.

Bom: Force feeds the thought. The harder you push, the harder it pushes back.

Yeon: Replace instead. Fill the evenings with things you'd pick anyway. Change one daily route. Archive the chat you keep rereading.

Bom: It won't stop in a day. But the gaps between thoughts get longer, and you'll notice.

Yeon: And the reason you push so hard? That's your blind spot. Next.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Shoving a thought out invites it back. Swap the habit instead. Boring. Works.

move_weak.text:
You said you want to stop thinking about them. Notice when the thoughts barge in. Tired, lonely, stretched thin. Almost never on a good day.

Bom: They're partly a sign your tank is low, not just that you miss them.

Yeon: So you'll get further protecting your battery than wrestling your brain.

Bom: Sleep, food, company, and less of whatever drains you. As you fill back up, the thoughts go quieter by themselves.

Yeon: Next, the blind spot that keeps draining you. Brace a little.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: The thoughts get loudest when you're running on empty. Refuel first.

unsure_strong.text:
You don't know what you want. For a strong chart, that feels like failing a test.

Yeon: It isn't. It's the start of a better decision than the fast one you'd normally make.

Bom: Give yourself a deadline that isn't tomorrow. A month.

Yeon: Until then, collect evidence. When do you miss them? When do you feel relief? Which future makes your shoulders drop?

Bom: At the end, look at the pile. It usually points somewhere.

Yeon: And the reason you hate not knowing? Blind spot. Next page.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Not knowing is allowed. Thirty days of notes, then decide.

unsure_weak.text:
You don't know what you want. That's completely okay, and honestly the most normal answer on this page.

Bom: With your chart, other people's opinions get loud enough to drown yours out. Of course it's foggy.

Yeon: Stop asking everyone. You've asked everyone.

Bom: Sit alone with it. Write "I want..." ten times and finish each one without editing.

Yeon: Some will be about them. Some won't. The ones that surprise you are the real answer.

Bom: Next, the blind spot that makes the fog thicker. Gently.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ten unedited sentences. The one that surprises you is the answer.

me.speaker: yeon
me.text: You said you ended it. And you're still here reading about them. Interesting.

them.speaker: bom
them.text: They ended it. So you didn't get a vote. That's a specific kind of hurt, and we'll be gentle with it.

mutual.speaker: yeon
mutual.text: "We both did, more or less." The "more or less" is doing a lot of work there.

unclear.speaker: bom
unclear.text: It faded out. No big fight, no clean ending. Those are the ones that stay open the longest.

unsaid.speaker: yeon
unsaid.text: You skipped who ended it. Which means the answer is complicated, or it still stings.

fresh.speaker: bom
fresh.text: Less than a month. Everything is still loud right now. Nothing you feel this week is a final answer.

months.speaker: yeon
months.text: One to six months. The "I'm totally fine" phase, followed by one song in a supermarket ruining your whole Thursday.

half.speaker: yeon
half.text: Six to twelve months, and they're still in your head rent-free. Time to look at the lease.

long.speaker: bom
long.text: Over a year. If it still pulls at you, it's not about missing them. It's about something they touched that's still open.

unsaid.speaker: yeon
unsaid.text: You didn't say how long. Which usually means "longer than I'd admit at brunch".

strength_titles.strong: Your blind spot: you push too hard
strength_titles.weak: Your blind spot: you give too much

sin-metal.why-it-ended:
You're a jewel. High standards, sharp eye, and you notice every little thing that's off. In love, that eye didn't switch off.

Yeon: You noticed every flaw. They noticed you noticing.

Bom: You also needed so much reassurance and asked for so little.

Yeon: So you tested them instead. Little silences. Little cold moments. To see if they'd chase.

Bom: It ended somewhere between your standards and your fear of not meeting theirs.
sin-metal.your-breakup-pattern:
Bom: And you break up beautifully. Composed. Gracious. Looking incredible the following week, which was not an accident.

Yeon: Meanwhile, inside, you're replaying details. What you wore. What you said. What you should have said, in a better font.

Bom: Your pattern is perfectionism about the ending itself. Needing to exit with dignity. Needing to know exactly where it went wrong.

Yeon: You may also be quietly judging yourself for choosing them in the first place.

Bom: Go easier. Picking someone who turned out wrong isn't bad taste. It's what happens to everyone who has a heart and uses it.
sin-metal.the-pull:
Be honest. You don't miss them. You miss the trailer. Who they were at their best. Who they were about to become.

Yeon: Any day now. Any day for two years.

Bom: You fall for the polished version. So you may miss the potential more than the actual person who left socks on the floor.

Yeon: And if they ended it, your pride wants a rematch. Just a small one. In a great outfit.

Bom: Work out which it is. If it's potential, remember potential isn't someone you can hold.

Yeon: If it's pride, the most elegant comeback is a life you genuinely enjoy. For you. Not for an audience of one.
sin-metal.the-honest-answer:
Nobody can read another person's decision from your birth date. That stays theirs. What's yours is your standard.

Yeon: You know your worth. You also sometimes accept less, so you won't look "difficult". Classic.

Bom: So instead of "will they come back", try this: would they meet the standard I actually have? The one I never said out loud?

Yeon: If no, the question answers itself.

Bom: If yes, the next step would be honest talk, including all the small hurts you swallowed to keep things pretty.

Yeon: A jewel isn't worth less for saying "that scratched".
sin-metal.if-they-reach-out:
If they get in touch, you'll want to write the perfect reply. Draft it. Then delete half.

Bom: You tend to over-polish and under-say. Work out what you actually feel, and write that. Plainly.

Yeon: Want to talk? Suggest it. Don't? A gracious short message is extremely you.

Bom: Watch for one thing: are they apologising for specifics, or just saying they miss you?

Yeon: Specifics matter to you. Let them matter. A vague "I miss us" is not a conversation about what happened. It's a vibe.
sin-metal.what-you-do-now:
Wear the thing. The one you've been saving for some imaginary better day. Today's the day. It's a Tuesday. Wear it.

Bom: You restore through beauty and order. Clean your space. Buy the flowers.

Yeon: Then do something where you're allowed to be bad. A beginner class. A messy art project. Karaoke, with a song you can't hit.

Bom: Spend time with people who make you laugh at yourself.

Yeon: Your sensitivity is a real strength. It just needs a break from scanning for flaws. Especially yours, which you find faster than anyone alive.

sin-metal.speaker: bom
sin-metal.text: You gave them the polished, beautiful version of you. That took effort.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: In the shower version, you win. Every time. Shame it's not on record.

sin-metal.speaker: bom
sin-metal.text: You feel things sharply. One careless sentence from them can still cut, months later.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: The outfit was perfect. The exit was perfect. You're still not okay. Both allowed.

sin-metal.speaker: bom
sin-metal.text: Your standards are fine. Saying them out loud is the new part.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: Best revenge? A great life. Not a reply with perfect punctuation.

spring.intro: A jewel born in spring. Everything was growing and you noticed all of it: what's pretty, what's off, what's three millimetres crooked. You have taste. You also have opinions about other people's taste.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You judged the font on their birthday card. Silently.

summer.intro: A jewel in summer heat. Pressure shaped you: to look good, do well, never be the embarrassing one. You're polished and impressive. One careless comment can still ruin your whole week.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You're allowed to be unfinished. It's charming, honestly.

autumn.intro: A jewel born in metal's own season. Double shine. High standards, sharp eye, zero patience for sloppy. You're the friend people dress up for. You're also the friend people are slightly scared to disappoint.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You're a five-star review. With a long comment section.

winter.intro: A jewel in winter water, washed clear. Your mind is quick and your words are precise. You can say one sentence that fixes everything, or one that ends everything. Most of the time you know which.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You see people so clearly. Use it to be kind.

earth.intro: A jewel still in the earth. Born in the soil weeks, so you were protected, maybe a little over-protected. You need to feel safe before you sparkle, and that's not a flaw. It's quality control.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You need three green flags before one selfie.

sin-metal.strong:
Your jewel is well set, Sin. Lots of support in your chart: sharp taste, high standards, a clear sense of your own worth.

Yeon: Which keeps you from settling. Great. It also turns breakups into a performance review. Of them.

Bom: Every flaw of theirs catalogued. Every mistake of yours locked in a drawer you don't open.

Yeon: And you're telling everyone you're entirely fine. In a very nice coat.

Bom: Blind spot: pride that won't let you be seen missing someone. If you're tempted to reach out, check whether it's love or wanting to win the final scene. You don't need the last word to shine.
sin-metal.weak:
Not much support around you in your chart, Sin. So your shine depends a lot on how other people see you.

Bom: In love you kept polishing to stay chosen. Right outfit. Right reply. Right mood. Every criticism landed as a scratch.

Yeon: Now you're reading their silence like a final grade. In red. With comments.

Bom: It isn't one. A jewel's worth doesn't drop because one person stopped looking.

Yeon: Spend time with people who rate you with no conditions. Practise being seen unpolished. Your value was never theirs to set.

after-hours.heading: The zoom-in
after-hours.text:
Your version of checking is a comparison. New photo up. You zoom in. Lighting, outfit, the new person if there is one. Do they look happier than they did with you?

Yeon: You zoomed in on a reflection in a window, Sin. We saw.

Bom: A jewel notices every flaw, especially the ones it suspects in itself. That's why this stings more than it should. Every look turns into a little verdict on you.

Yeon: Swap it. When the urge hits, open a note called "What I'm proud of this month" and add one thing instead.

Bom: Tiny counts. Finished a hard task. Said no. Wore the good shoes on a Tuesday.

Yeon: Attention is what polishes you. Give it to your own shine, not their feed.

Bom: Next: the balance in your chart. It explains why every look feels like a grade.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Their lighting is not your business anymore, Sin. Yours, however, is excellent.

four-weeks.heading: Four weeks of polish (and mess)
four-weeks.text:
Week one: refine one thing in your space. Clear a shelf. Frame a print. Buy one really good towel.

Bom: You recover through beauty and order. Small, precise, yours.

Week two: spend time near actual water. A swim, a river walk, a long bath with the phone in another room.

Yeon: In saju, Water is what polishes your metal. Also baths are nice. Both things are true.

Week three: say one thing you want, directly, to someone who matters. You tend to wait to be noticed instead of asking. The waiting is where the hurt grows.

Week four: let something be imperfect on purpose. Send the message without rereading it five times. Post the slightly blurry photo.

Bom: By the end of the month your standards are still high. You're just easier on yourself, and a jewel that isn't inspecting itself catches far more light.

Yeon: The blurry photo will be your favourite. Watch.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Spend time near water this month, Sin. It suits you.

first-message.heading: Replies, polished once
first-message.text:
Scripts, Sin. Written for a jewel that stays clear.

Bom: If you want to talk: "It's nice to hear from you. I'd like to talk. I'll be honest about what I need, and I hope you will be too."

Yeon: If you want distance: "Thank you for your message. I'm keeping some distance for now, and I wish you well."

Bom: If you're unsure: "I appreciate you writing. I'd like some time before I answer."

Yeon: What to avoid: the perfect reply. Drafted twelve times until it sounds effortless. It won't sound effortless. It'll sound drafted.

Bom: Polish once. Send. And notice whether you're answering to be chosen, or to choose.

Yeon: You can decide what you want before you find out if they still want you. Order matters.

Bom: Last chapter next. Bring the good shoes.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Draft two sounds like you. Draft twelve sounds like your lawyer.

sin-metal.title: You've replayed the last conversation forty times. With edits.
sin-metal.text:
You know exactly what you should have said. You've written it in your head, polished it, delivered it to an imaginary them in the shower. Perfect every time.

Bom: You want to get it right.

Yeon: You want to win a conversation that ended in March.
sin-metal.end: Yeon: The real reason it ended isn't in that conversation, by the way. It's on the next page.

cliff.sin-metal: Yeon: Your breakup pattern, Jewel: you leave a tiny bit early, so | nobody ever gets the chance to leave you first.

sin-metal.speaker: yeon
sin-metal.text: If they reach out, don't draft for an hour. The perfect reply is the one that sounds like you.

gap-wood-and-sin-metal.title: They rewrote the text three times. You sent a thumbs up.
gap-wood-and-sin-metal.you_are_a:
Your ex noticed every flaw and mentioned about a third of them. Beautifully phrased. Which somehow made it worse.

Yeon: The crease in your shirt. How you told that story at dinner. Your "ok 👍" to a message they'd clearly rewritten three times.

Bom: You think effort is just normal, so you never praised it. They wanted their effort seen. Every time. Specifically.

Yeon: You were blunt in public. They found it mortifying. You found their mortification dramatic.

Bom: Different currencies, real love. The exchange rate was the problem.

Yeon: Next time: when someone clearly tried, say what you noticed. "That dinner was perfect." Out loud. With your face.

Bom: And if they write again? Next page.
gap-wood-and-sin-metal.you_are_b:
You put care into every message and got "ok 👍" back.

Bom: You rewrote texts to get the tone right. You planned the dinner. You chose the gift with real thought.

Yeon: And they took it all as normal, because to them effort is just what decent people do. No praise. You noticed. Every time.

Bom: Then you'd say something precise about their shirt, or how they talked over the waiter, and they heard judgment where you meant care.

Yeon: You were both waiting to be appreciated in a language the other one didn't speak.

Bom: Asking for specific praise plainly isn't needy. "Did you notice I booked your favourite place?" is allowed.

Yeon: And if they text? Next page. Polish it once.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin, you wanted specific praise. Asking for it plainly isn't needy.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, "ok thumbs up" to a carefully written text should be illegal.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Real love, different currencies. Nobody brought a converter.

0.speaker: bom
0.text: Sin wanted specific praise. Asking for it plainly isn't needy.

1.speaker: yeon
1.text: Gap's "ok thumbs up" to a carefully written text should be illegal.

eul-wood-and-sin-metal.title: Each little note felt like a snip
eul-wood-and-sin-metal.you_are_a:
You were with someone who thought they were helping you grow the right way.

Bom: They had taste and precision, and an eye for detail you admired. And they aimed it at you.

Yeon: A comment about your outfit. A suggestion about your friend. A small edit to how you told a story.

Bom: Each one minor. Each one beautifully phrased. Each one a snip.

Yeon: You adapted, because adapting is what vines do. And they respected you a little less for it. Brutal, but true.

Bom: You're not a bonsai. You don't have to let people shape you.

Yeon: Next time, try "I like it this way." Then don't change it.

Bom: And if they message? Next page.
eul-wood-and-sin-metal.you_are_b:
You loved a beautiful plant and couldn't stop trimming it.

Bom: They were warm, adaptable, easy to love. And you saw everything they could be, with just a few adjustments.
